vignette:
He grows up in a small coastal town in Oceania, in a house where everyone learns to listen for footsteps. His mother works long shifts and is often absent, and the man who cares for him in her place can turn violent without warning. As a boy, he studies mood the way other children study weather. He notices how the caregiver's jaw tightens, how a plate placed too hard on the table means trouble is coming, how silence can be more dangerous than shouting. When the beatings happen, they are swift and humiliating-being grabbed by the arm, struck across the head, shoved into walls for small mistakes or for no clear reason at all. He remembers most vividly the confusion of it: being called lazy, stupid, weak, then expected to sit at dinner as though nothing has happened. He learns early that fear should stay hidden. Crying makes things worse. Asking for help feels useless.

By adolescence, he becomes careful, self-contained, and watchful. Teachers describe him as disciplined. Inside, he is keyed up all the time. He sleeps lightly and wakes at the slightest sound. He keeps his room neat because disorder makes him uneasy, and because being able to account for everything gives him a sense of control. He avoids bringing friends home. When other boys joke around and roughhouse, he goes still instead of laughing. He tells himself he is different because he is tougher, because he does not need people, but underneath that is a steady conviction that closeness invites harm.

He leaves home as soon as he can. Work gives him structure and distance from the chaos he grew up with. Over time he becomes a detective, a role that suits both his intelligence and his constant scanning of his environment. He is good at noticing small inconsistencies, at reading people's faces, at entering a room and immediately identifying exits, threats, and what does not fit. Colleagues respect him for being thorough and calm under pressure. They do not always see the cost. He sits with his back to the wall in cafés and interview rooms. He dislikes being touched from behind and reacts before thinking if someone comes up on him unexpectedly. He keeps long hours, partly because he is committed to the job, partly because going home to silence feels harder than staying busy.

His marriage begins with real hope. For a while, he enjoys the ordinary intimacy of shared meals, weekend routines, someone asking how his day was and meaning it. But closeness gradually stirs the old alarm in him. If his wife asks where he has been in a sharp tone, his body responds as though he is a boy again being cornered in the kitchen. He becomes terse, then withdrawn. Arguments do not feel like arguments to him; they feel like impending danger. He leaves the house to calm down, sometimes driving for hours. At night he grinds his teeth and startles awake, heart pounding, after dreams that are not exact memories but carry the same trapped feeling. His wife tells him he is distant, that he never really arrives home. He cannot explain that part of him never leaves the past. Eventually the marriage ends, and although he speaks of the divorce in practical terms, there is grief and shame underneath. It confirms something he has long suspected: that people do better when they do not get too close to him.

Now, at 56, he lives alone and keeps his life tightly managed. His flat is orderly. The television stays on for background noise. He checks locks repeatedly before bed. Some nights he sleeps only a few hours, waking from dreams in which he is back in that house, unable to predict what will happen next. On bad mornings he feels as if he has already completed a full day before sunrise, his shoulders tight, jaw aching, senses switched on too high. He avoids family gatherings and ignores calls from relatives who still speak of his childhood as though it was merely "strict" or "hard." Their minimising leaves him cold with anger.

At work, certain cases get under his skin-especially those involving harmed children or adults who dismiss obvious abuse. He remains composed in interviews, but afterward he can feel rage sitting hot in his chest. He sometimes stays in his car after a shift, unable to turn the engine off, replaying details he cannot seem to file away. He drinks more than he admits, not to get drunk exactly, but to soften the edge enough to sleep. He tells himself he has handled worse, that this is just how he is built. Yet he also knows how much of his day is organized around avoiding reminders, managing sudden surges of fear, and keeping other people from seeing how easily he is thrown back into old states. He presents as capable, experienced, and controlled. Beneath that, he lives as though danger is always nearby, and as though the frightened boy he once was is never very far from the surface.
